answers.1: Four object kinds: blob (one file's content, without its name), tree (one directory: names, modes and the IDs of its entries), commit (root tree ID, parent IDs, author, time, message) and tag (annotated: tagger, message, points to one object). There are also refs (HEAD, main). Refs are names that point to objects; they are not objects themselves. Every object is stored under its ID, which is the hash of its content.
answers.2: A ref points to a commit (HEAD → main → commit 7f3a…). A commit points to one root tree and to zero, one or several parent commits. A tree maps names to blobs (files) or to other trees (subdirectories). A blob points to nothing. A tag points to one object, usually a commit. Because the ID comes from the content, trees in different commits can point to the same blob or tree. In the diagram, both root trees point to README blob a3f2….
answers.3: An object's ID is the hash of its content, so identical content means one shared stored object. Changing a file creates a new blob ID. That changes the content, and so the ID, of every tree above it, up to the root tree and then the commit.
answers.4: The key variable is a file's content. If it changes, its blob gets a new ID. Each parent tree stores that ID, so each parent tree's content and ID change too, all the way up to the root tree and the commit. Siblings that did not change keep their IDs and are reused. If the content stays the same, the ID stays the same and nothing new is stored.
answers.5: Simplification: 'Hashes are shortened and made up' in the diagram. The diagram also leaves out the tag object. Established fact: 'Git stores each object under its ID, the hash of its content. Same content gives the same ID.' Also: `git show` computes the diff against the parent only when you ask for it.
answers.6: Git does not store a commit as a diff. A commit points to a complete root tree, which is a snapshot of the whole project. Trees map names to blobs (file contents) and to subtrees, and each object is stored under the hash of its content. So unchanged files and directories have the same IDs and are simply reused. A changed file gets a new blob, and new IDs ripple up through each parent tree to the root tree and the commit. Diffs are computed on demand, and packfile compression is a storage detail, not what a commit means.
answers.7: The hardest part was step 5: how a new ID ripples upward. It was clear for one level (src/), but the reader has to infer it for deeper nesting. Showing a second subdirectory that did not change would make the contrast clear: an unchanged subtree being shared, not only a blob. A short sentence on what a 'hash' is would also help, because the whole argument rests on 'same content → same ID'.
answers.8: A snapshot. The commit points to a whole tree. Diffs are computed on demand, for example by `git show`.
answers.9: It points to the same blob, the one with the same ID as in the first commit, as README.md → a3f2… does in both trees. If the unchanged item is a whole directory, the text implies (but does not show) that the same subtree is reused.
answers.10: These get new IDs: the file's blob, every tree on the path from it up to the root (src/ and any intermediate directories, then the root tree) and the commit. Blobs and subtrees that did not change keep their IDs. The parent commit keeps its ID.
answers.11: An object is stored under the hash of its content. An unchanged file has the same content, so it has the same ID and is the same stored object. The new tree just stores that existing ID, and nothing new is written. On top of that, packfiles compress similar objects against each other, but the explanation does not quantify this.

reasons.5: It names the rendering's simplifications (shortened hashes, no tag object) and correctly states that content-addressing and diff-on-demand are facts. It does not cover the model's other epistemic distinctions: packfile deltas are an implementation detail (compression, not the data model), and the hash is SHA-1 by default with SHA-256 possible. Only part of the fact / implementation-detail split is covered.

reasons.11: The mechanism is correct: same content gives the same ID, and the new tree stores the existing blob ID. But the answer gives no concrete case with numbers, such as README.md pointing to blob a3f2… in both root trees. The only quantification it mentions is about packfiles, and it says that is not quantified. A full answer needs a concrete case, so this is partial.
